new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has Archi with an empty rule (qs-tier-2026-09-12) and no existing statements; Chumakina supplies the two-syllable left window and the 'dynamic' type. It agrees with the primary source already in our check folder (Kibrik et al. 1977, p. 264: stress only on syllable 1 or 2, not automatic; Kibrik 1999, p. 429: variable mobile dynamic stress limited to the first two syllables). The listed open copy (hebis) is only the handbook's TOC; Unpaywall reports the chapter closed, CORE record 283485242 has no full text, the OUP page is could not be reached by automated download, so the quote comes from Google Books snippets, not a full read of the chapter.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dynamic (Russian-like) stress confined to a left-edge window of the first two syllables; the chapter gives no rule for choosing between syllable 1 and 2, so placement within the window is left as a lexical property. The subsection is headed 'Stress and Tone' but the snippet shows only these two sentences before 7.2.4 begins; nothing on tone was visible.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned in the visible text
new_statements.identity_note: All works describe Archi of the village Archib (single-village language); no dialect split is mentioned. Borise's Archi paragraph rests on Mikailov 1967, Kibrik et al. 1977 and Kibrik 1994; Chumakina's sketch is her own Surrey fieldwork on the same variety.

new_statements.quote: In Archi, the first two syllables of a lexical word comprise the stress window. Stress placement in disyllabic nouns is determined by vowel height: the second syllable is only stressed if the vowel in it is non-high (a, o or e): dórki 'eyelid', zímzu 'ant', buwá 'mother', motól 'baby goat' (Mikailov 1967: 18; Kibrik et al. 1977: 266). However, in the oblique forms of monosyllabic and disyllabic nouns stress often targets the second syllable, regardless of vowel height: lo 'child.SG', lobúr 'child.PL' (Mikailov 1967: 20). If the morphological makeup of a word would cause it to have stress outside of the stress window, the pretonic vowel is syncopated: e.g. matlá 'baby goat.ERG' (< motolá) (Kibrik 1994: 305). In verbs, as a rule, stress stays on one of the root syllables: átis 'let_go.INF', ék'as 'choose.INF' (Mikailov 1967: 19).

new_statements.relation_note: Same two-syllable left window as Chumakina 2020 and Kibrik; adds a vowel-height rule for disyllabic nouns, morphological overrides, and the syncope mechanism. Note that Borise's source, Kodzasov in Kibrik et al. 1977 p. 266, presents the height effect only as a tendency ('оно уходит с узких гласных i и u в первом слоге') and denies that general rules exist, so Borise's 'determined by vowel height' is stronger than the primary.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two-syllable left-edge stress window. In disyllabic nouns the second syllable is stressed only when its vowel is non-high (a, o, e), otherwise the first; oblique noun forms often take second-syllable stress regardless of vowel height; when morphology would push stress past syllable 2 the pretonic vowel syncopates so stress stays in the window; verbs keep stress on a root syllable. Borise files Archi under quantity-sensitive stress-window systems (phonological factors within a window).
new_statements.exceptions: oblique forms of mono- and disyllabic nouns stressed on syllable 2 regardless of vowel height (lo / lobúr); pretonic syncope (matlá < motolá); verbs: stress on a root syllable
new_statements.identity_note: All works describe Archi of the village Archib (single-village language); no dialect split is mentioned. Borise's Archi paragraph rests on Mikailov 1967, Kibrik et al. 1977 and Kibrik 1994; Chumakina's sketch is her own Surrey fieldwork on the same variety.

readall_conflicts: One mild disagreement of degree, not of placement. All sources put Archi stress on the first or second syllable (a left-edge two-syllable window): Kibrik et al. 1977 p. 264 and Kibrik 1999 p. 429 (already in our check notes), Chumakina 2020 p. 284, and Borise 2020 p. 737. Kibrik et al. 1977 say the choice between syllables 1 and 2 is not predictable by phonetic rules and must be listed ('необходимо иметь готовые акцентуированные формы в словаре'), with vowel height only a tendency; Chumakina 2020 gives no rule at all; Borise 2020 (citing Mikailov 1967 and Kibrik et al. 1977: 266) states a vowel-height rule for disyllabic nouns (second syllable stressed only if non-high) plus morphological overrides. So Borise reads the height tendency as a phonological rule (weight/sonority-sensitive within the window) where the primary description calls it a tendency inside a lexically fixed system. No source mentions tone, secondary stress, or absence of stress.

audit.recode_to: Keep classification weight-hedged (weight-sensitive (tentative), left edge, two-syllable window). Re-anchor the deciding quote on the held primary (Kibrik et al. 1977 t.1: 264-267) and soften the the primary-stress rule: placement within the sigma1/sigma2 window is lexically listed (1977: 264, 267; Kodzasov 2003: 64 'only by means of lexical marking'), with the strong tendency that high vowels i,u and o in syllable 1 are unstressed and a/e in syllable 1 mostly keep stress; drop 'closure as tiebreaker' as a stated rule unless Kodzasov 1999 is obtained and says so.
